# pc-themepark-doc

**A byte-level documentation of *Theme Park* (Bullfrog Productions / Electronic
Arts, 1994), as a live GOG Galaxy installation on the owner's own machine.**
No game assets and no executables are in this repository — only measurements
and the code that reproduces them.

| | |
|---|---|
| **what** | *Theme Park*, DOS, 1994 — GOG gameId `1207660423`, buildId `58012507054984672` |
| **studio** | Bullfrog Productions, for Electronic Arts — read out of `LANG0-0.DAT`, not out of a database |
| **object** | 223 files, **187,015,187 bytes**, 184 distinct sha1, 14 directories |
| **verified** | size, mtime to the 100-nanosecond tick and sha1, **223 of 223** |
| **coverage** | free at the start **7.3995 %**; closed at **89.8992 %**, residue **0** |
| **the big one** | 17 animation files, 145,695,310 bytes, **77.9056 %** — all seventeen walked, all seventeen residue 0 |
| **the index** | 25 tables, two record shapes derived, **12 of 12** sound tables closing at residue 0, **345 named members** |
| **the programs** | three `LE` linear executables, **3 of 3 accounted to the byte**; DOS/4GW 1.97 built `May 19 1994 14:39:18` |
| **the state** | 19 save files, three parks, seven years, and one park saved twice three years apart |
| **crossings** | **11 of 184** at the file, **0 of 9,826** at the member |
| **new tools** | `bfflic.py`, `tptab.py`, `le.py`, `langtab.py`, `tpsave.py` — 1,546 lines, 38 selftest specimens, 23 of which must be refused |

## What was actually found

The object is 77.9056 % one animation format that declares Autodesk's FLC
magic and then declares a file size of **12**. Twelve is not a lie: **it is the
length of the header.** These are ordinary FLIC frame chains behind a
twelve-byte Bullfrog header, and walking them from offset 12 closes every one
of the seventeen files exactly.

Fifteen of them are **rides**, and they are named — by the game's own language
table, by a table inside every save file, and by a format string in the
executable, three witnesses that agree on one order of 29. `RIDEANI.004` is the
maze and is the largest file in the object; `RIDEANI.000` is the Flight Sim,
which is a cinema, and what is playing on its screen is the **Bullfrog
Productions logo followed by a title card reading `CARPET`** — *Magic Carpet*,
Bullfrog's own game of the same year, running inside a fairground ride.

And the park called `HORZA` carries the string `HORZA HAS JUST CHEATED!`, which
the owner's recollection predicted and the bytes confirmed. So does `DEMO.GY`,
the park Bullfrog shipped in the box.

## The chapters

| # | chapter | what is in it |
|---|---|---|
| [00](docs/00-predictions.md) | predictions | 66 clauses written before anything was opened, and the calibration series applied as a prior for the first time |
| [01](docs/01-the-object.md) | the object | five denominators, three in-or-out decisions with three different reasons, and the coverage |
| [02](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | the technical sheet | every figure with the command that makes it again, and what does not apply |
| [03](docs/03-the-seventeen.md) | the seventeen | the animation container, 17 of 17 at residue 0, and the one field that really is broken |
| [04](docs/04-the-rides.md) | the rides | fifteen of twenty-nine named, the fourteen gaps partitioned, and the logo in the cinema |
| [05](docs/05-the-index-and-the-pictures.md) | the index and the pictures | a 6-byte sprite record, a 32-byte named sound record, thirteen screens and nine 6-bit palettes |
| [06](docs/06-the-sound.md) | the sound | 345 named members, three synthesisers, fourteen adult voice lines and a bark |
| [07](docs/07-the-words.md) | the words | 1,142 strings in 26 groups, five languages, one reachable, and the credit roll |
| [08](docs/08-the-saves.md) | the saves | three parks, 88.1697 % zero, the cheat, and one park three years apart |
| [09](docs/09-the-programs.md) | the programs | three `LE` images, Watcom, DOS/4GW, and the decision about `hurlle.py` |
| [10](docs/10-the-accounting.md) | the accounting | twenty buckets, residue 0, and how much of 187 MB is actually 1994 |
| [11](docs/11-the-clocks.md) | the clocks | seven years of one person, and 1994 found only in other people's binaries |
| [12](docs/12-the-shop.md) | the shop | 195 declarations not 179, three witnesses one of them mute, and a prediction that closes |
| [13](docs/13-whose-bytes.md) | whose bytes | two controls that disagree, 2,403 addresses that are not addresses, and a play log |
| [14](docs/14-against-the-collection.md) | against the collection | 11 of 184, 0 of 9,826, and an extender that got everywhere |
| [15](docs/15-the-tools.md) | the tools | five written, two repaired, and a fifth defect that is now an argument about the tool |
| [16](docs/16-corrections.md) | corrections | eight in the pre-briefing, four of this session's own |
| [17](docs/17-leftovers.md) | leftovers | what is still closed, and twenty-one acronyms marked proved, attributed or not |
| [18](docs/18-prediction-scoring.md) | scoring | `inherited` 22.50/26, `open` 39.00/40, and the ninth consecutive negative |

## Nineteen documents, and why

The last ten sessions produced 19, 17, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 17 and 19.
This one produced **nineteen**, and two chapters that were planned separately
were merged because the subject merged, not because a number wanted them to:

* *what applies and what does not* is a section of **02** rather than its own
  chapter, because on an object with no optical media, no Unity, no PE32+ and
  no encryption the list of absent things is short and belongs beside the sheet
  it qualifies;
* *the index* and *the pictures* are one chapter (**05**) because the index
  points at the pictures: the same file that gives a sprite its width gives a
  screen its palette's name, and splitting them would have printed the
  `MSPR-0.TAB` record layout twice.

Two chapters that could have been merged were not. **04** is what the animations
*show* and **03** is how the container works, and they are different questions
about the same 145,695,310 bytes — one is a format and the other is a park.

## Reproducing anything here

```
python tools/hashall.py themepark-gog
python tools/bfflic.py census themepark-gog/GAME/DATA
python tools/tptab.py census themepark-gog/GAME/DATA
python tools/le.py info themepark-gog/GAME/MAIN.EXE
python tools/langtab.py --census themepark-gog/GAME/DATA
python tools/tpsave.py census themepark-gog
python tools/gogmanifest.py --root themepark-gog
python _work/accounting.py
```

Every tool takes the installation directory or a file under it. Nothing writes
into the object; nothing needs a key; nothing here needs the game to be run,
and the emulator that came with it was not launched.

**`notes/` holds the output of every command this repository quotes**, 33 files,
so a figure can be checked against the run that produced it without the object
being present. The chapters also cite `_work/*.py` — `accounting.py`,
`clocks.py`, `find1994.py`, `goglog.py`, `hashdb.py`, `screens.py`,
`witnesses.py`, `members.py`, `emailrate.py` — which are this session's one-off
scripts rather than tools, and which follow the convention of the four
repositories before this one: **the script is not published, its output is**,
in `notes/`. Where a script's job was to redact something before it could be
written down at all — `goglog.py` — the redaction is therefore visible in
`notes/goglog.txt` and the unredacted file never leaves the object.

vs-sr-dev-pc-landsoflore-doc-readme.text:
# Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos — PC/DOS, Westwood Studios, 1993/94

A byte-level study of a 325,758,928-byte GOG installation in which 94.17 % of
the bytes are one file, that file is a CD, the CD's volume descriptor is dated
**seventeen years after the game it contains**, and the same 34-byte directory
record appears four times inside it carrying three different dates.

Nothing here is emulation, patching or preservation advocacy. It is measurement:
every number carries the command that reproduces it, the sixty-one predictions
were written before a single file was opened and are scored whether they won or
lost, and the four container formats are described in the docstrings of the
tools that read them.

**The object is not in this repository and was never committed to it.** It is a
live GOG installation on a drive this repository does not own; **nothing in this
session wrote to that drive**. A verified working copy was made under an ignored
directory. One field belongs to the person who owns the installation — the
install path, which `goglog.ini` repeats five times — and is **redacted as `<G>`
everywhere in this repository. There is no other personal data: a search for
`C:\Users`, `Documents and Settings` and `/Users/` across all 65 installed files
**and the 209 files inside the disc image** returns nothing.

This is also the first object in the collection that is **openly the work of
three separate groups of people, twenty years apart**: Westwood Studios in
1992–1994, the DOSBox volunteers in the 2000s, and GOG in 2011. Every figure
below names the layer it belongs to, because a 2011 date in an ISO root is not
Westwood's mistake and a 1992 timestamp on a 9 KB library is not GOG's
achievement.

---

## The short card

| | |
|---|---|
| **title** | *Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos*, the CD revision. The disc calls itself **`LOL_V102`** — version 1.02 — in the one field designed to hold a name |
| **platform** | PC/**DOS**, real mode, 16-bit. Four `MZ` executables, seven video-driver overlays (`cga` `ega` `mga` `tga` `vga` `xga` `yga`), and two `LE` VxDs for an operating system the game does not run on |
| **the object** | **65 files, 5 directories, 325,758,928 bytes** — agreed to the byte by `du -sb` and by the sum of 65 `stat` calls |
| **the three layers** | **the game 33 files / 310,242,796 B / 95.24 %** · the emulator 14 / 5,883,321 / 1.81 % · the storefront 18 / 9,632,811 / 2.96 %. [01](docs/01-what-this-object-is.md) |
| **the studio** | **Westwood Studios**, and for the first time in this collection the object says so **in a field built for the purpose**: the `publisher` of the volume descriptor. It repeats it in `SETUP.EXE` (`Westwood Studios -- Lands of Lore`) and 38 times in `INSTALL.EXE`. It appears **zero** times in `MAIN.EXE` |
| **the disc** | `GAME.DAT` is an **ISO 9660 image**: 149,781 sectors of 2,048, two descriptors, no Joliet, no El Torito, **no HFS** — and the absence is measured, not assumed: the 32,768-byte system area is 32,768 zero bytes |
| **the sector map** | **149,753 file + 8 directory + 2 path table + 16 system area + 2 descriptors = 149,781. Zero sectors belong to nobody and zero belong to two things.** The first object in this collection to close exactly |
| **the clocks** | **four, and three of them are not the product's.** 209 file records say 1992–1994; the volume descriptor says **2011-09-13**; three storefront files say 2017 and 2019; the other 62 mtimes say the day of installation, inside a ten-second window |
| **the four copies** | the root directory's 34-byte record is written **four times** in the image and **all four disagree**: `1970-01-01T01:00:00` in the descriptor, `2011-09-13T11:39:37` twice in the root's own extent, and **all zero** in `DATA`'s parent record. [03](docs/03-the-volume-descriptor.md) |
| **the tell** | the **GMT-offset byte**. 224 of the 226 directory records carry `0`. The two that carry 2011 carry `8` — two quarter-hours times four, Central European Summer Time. **The timezone field is a map of what was edited in 2011**, and it is 104 bytes wide |
| **the speech** | **4,912 recorded lines in thirty `.TLK` files, 228,244,919 bytes, 70.07 % of the object.** Every one is a `Creative Voice File`: **8-bit unsigned PCM, mono, uncompressed**, at 22,222.22 Hz — not 22,050, because the rate is a one-byte time constant and the object states it exactly |
| **the running time** | **10,271.5636 seconds — 2 h 51 m 11.56 s** — summed from 4,912 declared block lengths with **zero samples decoded**. Counting the speech that lives outside the `.TLK` files as well: **5,508 recordings, 253,486,652 bytes, 3 h 12 m 11.50 s, 77.81 % of the object** |
| **the shape of the speech** | median line **1.907 s**, mean 2.091, longest **6.566 s**, and **not one line of 4,912 runs longer than seven seconds**. Lines, not monologues |
| **how it is addressed** | by number. A line is `001A0` in archive `22`; the member is named `001A0.22`. **Nothing in 4,912 names is a word** |
| **the archives** | **132 `.PAK`, 2,297 members, and all 132 close to the byte.** The `.TLK` files are the same format with a different extension: **7,209 members in total, every one an 8.3 upper-case name, none containing a path separator** |
| **the format correction** | the archive terminator is **nine bytes, not five** — offset, empty name, and a zero `uint32` nobody mentions. 132 of 132 disagree with the five-byte reading by exactly four bytes |
| **the game, three times** | the installed game is a copy of files inside the image; **`WESTWOOD.001` is a third copy of twenty-one of them**, inside the image, in a fourth container format; and 17 loose `.ADL` are members of an archive inside the image. `dupes.py` sees **64,230 bytes** of this. The truth is **3,491,298** loose, and **128,461,128 across all 7,504 leaves — 20.449 %** |
| **the ten bytes** | of the 32 loose Westwood files, **31 exist inside the image and one does not**: `LANDS.CFG`, 10 bytes. It is the only byte of the game layer that the installation itself wrote |
| **the translation** | the three language trees are 60,518,486 bytes and **57.76 % of that is the same content three times**. One level down, **368 of 377 archive members are byte-identical across all three languages**: translating this game costs **142,617 bytes — 0.739 %** |
| **the only source tree** | `WESTWOOD.001` opens with a 612-byte `files.lst` naming every file's path **on the machine that built the CD in 1994**: `\projects\lol_cd\project\run\voc.pak`, `master.002\data\hardrive\main.exe`. The inherited path scanner found none of it |
| **absolute paths** | `MAIN.EXE`, `MAINW.EXE`, `SETUP.EXE`, `LOLCD.EXE`: **zero**, as in 1990 and 1992. `DOSBox.exe`, 3.8 MB compiled by volunteers in 2010: **zero**. The one build-machine path in the game layer is in a **text-editor session file** left in the French directory, and it names `r:\intro\td.bat` three times |
| **the two executables** | `MAIN.EXE` and `MAINW.EXE` differ by 4,272 bytes and **69.18 % of the smaller is byte-identical to the larger**, found by `crossmatch.py` unmodified. Neither is compressed and neither is a Windows binary |
| **the oldest byte** | `WESTWOOD.DLL`, 1992-06-11, and it is not Westwood's: it is an `NE` Windows library built with **Borland C++ 1991**, a *"Meter Custom Control Library"* — a progress bar |
| **the vendor named in a binary** | **`Copyright (C) 1991,1992 Miles Design, Inc.`**, in six `.ADV` sound drivers. In 2014 the equivalent was RAD Game Tools |
| **the verifier** | `goggame-1207662513.hashdb` is a ZIP holding **35 records of 1,056 bytes — a 1,024-byte name and a 32-character MD5**. All 35 verify. It is the first descriptor in this collection that can be **wrong**, and what it covers is the point: **the 33 files of the game, the manual and the icon. Not the emulator, not the installer, not itself** |
| **the emulator's knowledge** | the fifteen DOSBox files name *Lands of Lore* **zero** times. `dosbox-0.74-2.1.tar.gz` is the real source — 346 members, `src/dosbox.cpp`, `COPYING` — and it is a **GPL obligation, not a leftover** |
| **leftovers** | **502,100 bytes — 0.1541 % of the object** — and **99.96 % of it belongs to the two groups who did not make the game**. Westwood's share is **187 bytes**: a programmer's text-editor session left in the French directory, naming a batch file on drive `R:` three times. Counted apart: **28.670 % of the disc** is content the disc already carries elsewhere, and none of that is a mistake |
| **where this stops** | the pixel formats. `.WSA`, `.CPS`, `.SHP`, `.VCN`, `.TIM`, `.FNT`, `.PCS`, `.VMP`, `.PAL`, `.WLL`, `.CMZ`, `.COL` — **1,356 members and 44,006,858 bytes, 13.509 % of the object** — are named, counted and **not decoded**. [15](docs/15-where-i-stop.md) says what opening them would take |
| **predictions** | 61 clauses plus 3 named inferences, written before a file was opened: **48 hit, 3 half, 13 miss = 77.3 %** (method 88.9 %, content 75.5 %). Seven of the thirteen misses are one error: assuming that things which resemble each other were made the same way |

Everything above is derived in the chapters and every figure has a command.

---

## The chapters

| | |
|---|---|
| [00 — the predictions](docs/00-predictions.md) | sixty-one bets placed before a single file was opened |
| [01 — what this object is](docs/01-what-this-object-is.md) | three groups of people, twenty years apart, one directory |
| [02 — the spec sheet](docs/02-spec-sheet.md) | every figure with the command that reproduces it |
| [03 — the volume descriptor](docs/03-the-volume-descriptor.md) | the fourth answer, the first that is really a disc, and the four copies that disagree |
| [04 — the clocks](docs/04-the-clocks.md) | four of them, and three are not the product's |
| [05 — the disc](docs/05-the-disc.md) | 149,781 sectors and not one of them belongs to nobody |
| [06 — the speech](docs/06-the-speech.md) | 4,912 lines, two hours fifty-one, and not a word in any name |
| [07 — the archives](docs/07-the-archives.md) | 132 that close, and a terminator four bytes longer than described |
| [08 — the game three times](docs/08-the-game-three-times.md) | duplication at three levels, and the ten bytes that are only in one |
| [09 — the three languages](docs/09-the-three-languages.md) | what a translation costs, measured one level down |
| [10 — the executables](docs/10-the-executables.md) | two builds 4,272 bytes apart, and the progress bar from 1991 |
| [11 — the installer](docs/11-the-installer.md) | a fourth container, and the only source tree on the disc |
| [12 — the emulator](docs/12-the-emulator.md) | 5,883,321 bytes that have never heard of this game |
| [13 — the storefront](docs/13-the-storefront.md) | the first descriptor in this collection that can be wrong |
| [14 — against the echo](docs/14-against-the-echo.md) | yesterday's object was 83 % performance and so is this one, and two points are not a curve |
| [15 — where I stop](docs/15-where-i-stop.md) | four codecs written, three that close, and one frame in three that does not |
| [16 — the leftovers](docs/16-the-leftovers.md) | three columns, because three groups left them |
| [17 — the tools](docs/17-tools.md) | five inherited unmodified, one that answered politely and wrongly, twelve written |
| [18 — open questions](docs/18-open-questions.md) | one closed on an object that did not ask it, and eight still open |
| [19 — corrections](docs/19-corrections.md) | eleven of mine and six of the briefing's |
| [20 — prediction scoring](docs/20-prediction-scoring.md) | every clause, scored, including the six that were wrong for one reason |

vs-sr-dev-pc-sargon5-doc-readme.text:
# pc-sargon5-doc

Reverse-engineering notes on **Sargon V: World Class Chess** (Mediagenic, 1991)
— the last of the line Dan and Kathe Spracklen started in 1978 with a Z80
program written for a computer chess tournament, and the only one whose PC
front end this repository is about.

The About box splits the credit itself:

```
Chess Engine: Dan & Kathe Spracklen
P.C. Engine: Kevin E. Leavelle
```

Everything here is the second half — the container, the codec, the display
layer, the position records, the tutorial system. The search itself is a black
box this project has not opened.

**Documentation only.** No game assets, no extracted art, no audio, no
executable code is committed here. The tools in [`tools/`](tools/) reproduce
every figure, table and image from your own legally obtained copy.

## What is documented

| Doc | Contents |
|---|---|
| [00-overview.md](docs/00-overview.md) | The release, the two disagreeing copyright lines, the eight shipped files |
| [01-executable.md](docs/01-executable.md) | `SARGON5.EXE`: the LZEXE wrapper, the 32-copy copyright fence, the data segment, the command line, EMS, the build |
| [02-container-and-codec.md](docs/02-container-and-codec.md) | The 16-byte directory and the LSB-first LZW that five of the eight files share |
| [03-graphics.md](docs/03-graphics.md) | `SCREENE.HUH`: eight frames, 182 sprites, the bottom-centre anchor, the piece-set loader |
| [04-palettes-and-16-colour.md](docs/04-palettes-and-16-colour.md) | The VGA palette and the 768-byte table that lets one asset set serve four displays |
| [05-fonts.md](docs/05-fonts.md) | `FONTS.FNT`: six proportional faces, and the tail of the character range |
| [06-display-drivers.md](docs/06-display-drivers.md) | `WAZZOO.DRV`: VGA, EGA, Tandy — and a register-level Tandy 1000 SL/TL driver |
| [07-audio.md](docs/07-audio.md) | Six standard MIDI files, seven device records, and the card with no switch |
| [08-opening-book.md](docs/08-opening-book.md) | `OPENE.BOK`: 338 opening names, and what can be said about the tree |
| [09-position-records.md](docs/09-position-records.md) | The 512-byte record every game, lesson and puzzle uses; the move stream |
| [10-annotated-lessons.md](docs/10-annotated-lessons.md) | `.ANN` coaching trees, and the `.ANT` sources that shipped by accident |
| [11-text-board-format.md](docs/11-text-board-format.md) | The plain-text board importer nothing in the release uses |
| [12-easter-eggs-and-leftovers.md](docs/12-easter-eggs-and-leftovers.md) | Dr. Destructo, Hamster Gone Bad Productions, and what happens to the white king |
| [13-open-questions.md](docs/13-open-questions.md) | Everything unresolved, with the measurements behind it |
| [notes/resource-inventory.md](notes/resource-inventory.md) | All 219 blocks across the five containers, grouped and sized |
| [notes/tutorial-inventory.md](notes/tutorial-inventory.md) | 335 lessons and games, the two numbering gaps, the census |
| [notes/string-inventory.md](notes/string-inventory.md) | The credits, the messages, the file names, the device names |

## Highlights

**Five files with four different extensions are one format.** `SCREENE.HUH`,
`SMORE.HUH`, `FONTS.FNT`, `WAZZOO.DRV` and `OPENE.BOK` share a directory of
16-byte entries with no magic number, no signature and no entry count — the
first entry's data offset *is* the directory length, so the count is that
offset divided by sixteen. All 219 blocks across the five files are contiguous,
and every one decodes to exactly its declared size.

**The codec is LZW read backwards.** Nine to twelve bits, 256 clear, 257 end —
and packed **least-significant bit first**, where GIF, TIFF and Unix `compress`
all pack MSB-first. Attacking the first block the usual way is not obviously
wrong: it runs, and produces 955 plausible bytes before the dictionary walks
off. Read the same bytes LSB-first and it lands on exactly 64,000 — one 320×200
frame. On an 8086 the LSB-first accumulator is a shift and a mask; MSB-first
needs a rotate through a width that changes under you.

**One asset set serves four displays.** There is no EGA art and no Tandy art in
the release. Every sprite and every screen is 8-bit indexed, and each palette
block carries 768 bytes of VGA DAC values *plus* 768 more — three bytes, six
nibbles per colour — that express the same 256 colours for the 16-colour
drivers. Substitute any one of those six nibble planes for the whole image and
the picture stays legible. That single decision is why the sprites are chunky
rather than planar and why the EGA driver is the biggest of the four.

**WAZZOO.DRV is video, not audio.** Four blocks, thirty entry points each —
one interface, four implementations. Driver 1 is the one worth reading: it
never calls the BIOS, and instead writes nineteen 6845 CRTC registers, five
video-array registers through 0x3DA/0x3DE, and a page register at 0x3DF before
clearing 64,000 bytes at A000. That is **Tandy 1000 SL/TL 640×200 in 16
colours**, programmed by hand, as a separate driver from the ordinary Tandy
one. Somebody on the team had the machine.

**Every game, lesson, puzzle and endgame is the same 512-byte record.** Four
extensions — `.SAR`, `.ILL`, `.CMB`, `.ENG` — and one format: a 256-byte move
stream, then a 32-slot piece list of types and 0x88 squares that is never
compacted, so a captured man keeps its slot and gets square 0x80. The trailer's
one interesting byte is a **cursor**, not a length: `class013.sar` has a
63-byte stream with the cursor at 16, so 47 bytes of that game are recorded but
not yet played. The shipped saved games are recordings wound back, not
truncated.

**The move stream is one byte per half-move, and the opening statistics decode
it.** Bit 7 is the side; the low seven bits are a 1-based index into the move
list the engine generates. 113 records start from the initial position, and
their first byte takes exactly four values — 12 (80 times), 14 (26), 1 (4),
16 (3). Those are 1.e4, 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4, in the right proportions. The
second byte takes nine values, which come out as e5, c5, Nf6, d5, e6, d6, c6,
f5 and Nh6 — the Sicilian, the Indian defences, the Queen's Gambit, the French,
the Pirc, the Caro-Kann and the Dutch, again in the right proportions. The
generator emits knight moves first, king's knight before queen's, then pawns
from the h-file to the a-file, one-square push before two. Where it stops is in
[chapter 13](docs/13-open-questions.md), stated with the number: a replay gets
2,290 of 4,631 half-moves.

**A tutorial lesson is a decision tree, not a recording.** `sicw.ann` carries
318 move entries for a twenty-turn game. Twenty are the correct moves, twenty
the machine's replies, twenty a catch-all — and the other 258 are anticipated
mistakes, each with its own sentence. Turn 1 of `frenchb.ann` names four rival
openings by the first move that gives them away; turn 3 enumerates twenty-six
wrong moves, including every pawn advance on the board under one message,
*"A waste of a precious move"*.

**The lessons' source code shipped, and the game cannot see it.** `WHITE.ANT`
and `BLACK.ANT` are the plain-text authoring format the `.ANN` files were
compiled from — move lines, wildcards, `XXX` as a section break. The file
dialog filters on `*.ANN`. Two authoring files, in the retail game directory,
invisible to the program that shipped them. The typo in *"a sample black
anotated game"* is in the retail file.

**There is a plain-text board importer nobody used.** A routine at 0x16CED
accepts a file that begins with a plus sign, reads a two-character piece code
every five bytes and every 86 bytes a new rank, matching against
`WPWRWBWNWKWQBPBRBBBNBKBQ` plus two spaces for empty. Every constant in it
resolves to an ASCII board drawn with `+----+` separators and `| BR |` cells,
CRLF throughout. No `.TXT` ships, nothing demonstrates it, and it is strict
enough that one character out of place rejects the file.

**The programmer is credited as "Dr. Destructo".** Four of the thirteen job
titles in the About box are jokes — *Interloper*, *Cool Boss*, *Grunt-work* —
but only one replaces a person's name, on the line directly under Dan and Kathe
Spracklen.

**Hold `h` while the About box is open.** A sprite appears at (210, 163) and
two lines of text at (154, 87): **Hamster Gone Bad / Productions!** The routine
is the About dialog's own draw procedure, it checks the keyboard state array
for ASCII `h`, and each time it fires it increments a counter. Do it three
times, then hold `q` in two further dialogs, and a hook inside the piece-set
loader comes alive: on the **fifth** of the twelve sprites it loads — the
**white king** — it substitutes block 192 or block 193 instead. Which one is
decided by a sixteen-bit LFSR with taps 0xB400, one time in four. Block 193 is
a digitised bespectacled human face. Block 192 is a hamster holding something
that has nothing to do with chess. Either of them then plays the game as
White's king.

**A card with a driver and no switch.** The executable carries seven audio
device records: AdLib, IBM PS/1, Roland MT-32, Internal Speaker, Tandy 1000,
Null Device — and **Game Blaster PC Music Board**, Creative's 1987 CMS card,
which no command-line switch selects and the help box never lists. Conversely
there is no "Sound Blaster" string anywhere in the image: `/S` reaches the
AdLib record, because a Sound Blaster's music side *is* an OPL2.

**Two numbering gaps ship in the retail data.** `end22.eng` is missing from an
otherwise unbroken 1–58, and `opngs007` through `opngs010` from 1–69. The
surrounding files are present and intact.

## Tools

Pure Python 3. `pillow` is needed for the rendering paths and `capstone` only
for the driver disassembler.

```
tools/s5lib.py       the container, the LZW, sprites, palettes
tools/s5res.py       list, verify and extract any container
tools/s5gfx.py       screens, sprite sheets, piece sets, the 16-colour test
tools/s5font.py      FONTS.FNT
tools/s5drv.py       the four display drivers
tools/s5music.py     the six MIDI files
tools/s5book.py      OPENE.BOK and its 338 opening names
tools/s5pos.py       positions from .SAR, .ILL, .CMB and .ENG, as diagrams and FEN
tools/s5ann.py       .ANN lessons, as readable coaching transcripts
tools/s5unpack.py    the LZEXE 0.91 wrapper
tools/s5strings.py   text out of the unpacked image
tools/s5export.py    one shot: all of the above into one directory
```

```sh
python tools/s5export.py "<install>" ./out
```

or piecemeal:

```sh
python tools/s5res.py    "<install>" verify
python tools/s5res.py    "<install>" list SCREENE.HUH
python tools/s5gfx.py    "<install>" screens ./screens
python tools/s5gfx.py    "<install>" pieces piece-sets.png
python tools/s5gfx.py    "<install>" ega 20 title-16.png
python tools/s5font.py   "<install>" sheet fonts.png
python tools/s5drv.py    "<install>" info
python tools/s5music.py  "<install>" dump ./music
python tools/s5book.py   "<install>" names
python tools/s5pos.py    board "<install>/tutorial/bg01.cmb"
python tools/s5ann.py    text  "<install>/tutorial/frenchb.ann"
python tools/s5unpack.py "<install>" s5.bin
python tools/s5strings.py s5.bin
```

`<install>` is the directory holding `SARGON5.EXE`, with `games/` and
`tutorial/` beside it.

## Status

The container and its codec are solved and verified block by block — all 219
of them, across all five files. `SCREENE.HUH`, `FONTS.FNT`, `SMORE.HUH` and
`WAZZOO.DRV` are decoded end to end. The 512-byte position record is solved
except for the move stream's generator ordering, which is decoded far enough to
read every opening move in the corpus and no further. The opening book's tree
is not decoded. [Chapter 13](docs/13-open-questions.md) lists all of it, with
the numbers.

# Plundered Hearts — MS-DOS, Infocom, 1987

A byte-level study of **five files and 146,252 bytes**, in which a
twelve-kilobyte virtual machine runs a game ten point seven times its own size,
**88.18 % of the object is language and 0 % of it is a recording**, the
publisher's name appears four times and only in five-bit compressed characters,
the author's name appears nowhere at all, and a sixty-four-byte header from 1987
verifies its own contents with two bytes.

Nothing here is emulation, patching or preservation advocacy. It is
measurement: every number carries the command that reproduces it, the
sixty-six predictions were written before a Z-string was decoded and are scored
whether they won or lost, and the format is described in the docstrings of the
tools that read it.

**Nothing of the object is in this repository.** The five files were copied into
this directory to be read, and `.gitignore` excludes them by directory name
before it excludes them by extension. `git ls-files` is verified line by line
before every commit. There is **one** piece of personal data in the object — a
private postal address, in the shareware banner of a console driver that has
nothing to do with the game — and it is **not transcribed anywhere in this
repository**, including in `notes/`. That it exists is recorded; what it says is
not.

The rule this document was written under, and the way it could have failed:
*having opened everything, to narrate instead of measuring.* The briefing that
began this session had already opened the whole header, the whole string pool,
the driver banner and the batch file. Everything below is what was measured
afterwards.

---

## The short card

| | |
|---|---|
| **title** | *Plundered Hearts*, the MS-DOS edition. The object names its publisher — `Copyright (c) 1987 by Infocom, Inc.` — **only in compressed text**, four times, and never in ASCII |
| **platform** | MS-DOS, real mode. Two `.COM` files, no `MZ`, no relocation; the game itself is not 8086 code at all but a **Z-machine version 3** program |
| **the object** | **5 files, 146,252 bytes.** No sixth file, no hidden file, no alternate data stream |
| **the layers** | story file **88.1786 %** · interpreter 8.2078 % · a third-party console driver **3.5699 %** · a batch file 0.0417 % · a 3-byte config 0.0021 % |
| **the date** | **1987-07-30**, from the header's `serial` field. Four files say 1996, one says 2001. The filesystem does not date this product; **the product dates itself** |
| **the descriptor** | the eighth answer to this collection's oldest open question: a 64-byte header that declares its length and a 16-bit sum of every byte from `0x40` to it. **Declared `0x406D`, computed `0x406D`** — and the same six 8086 instructions inside the interpreter compute it the same way. [03](docs/03-the-header.md) |
| **content verification** | the *verifies content* row now reads **1987 → 1999 → 2011**. Not something distribution invented when files got large: what you do when a floppy might be bad |
| **the byte the checksum cannot see** | the file is 128,963 bytes and declares 128,962. The extra one is **`0x1A`**, a DOS end-of-file marker left by a text-mode copy. The descriptor excludes it by construction |
| **the alphabet** | derived from the story file in five steps — an exact tiling, a frequency split, a monotone bijection, and three characters pinned by the dictionary's raw separator bytes — then checked against the 78 characters printed inside the interpreter. **78 of 78 agree.** [06](docs/06-the-alphabet.md) |
| **the unit** | **18,701 words.** 2,391 prose strings, 101,368 characters, in 66,350 stored bytes, decoded from every string in all five populations |
| **where the text hides** | 343 packed strings are **16.7 %** of it. The other 2,048 are **inline inside `print` instructions**, which is why finding them needed a disassembler |
| **the packing** | 1.3627 characters per byte from the five-bit encoding; **1.6197** with abbreviations. In ASCII the story file would be 170,080 bytes instead of 128,963 |
| **the abbreviations** | 96 entries, **all used, 9,735 times, no duplicates**, saving **12,158 bytes = 9.4275 %** net of their own 610-byte cost. The most-used is not a word: it is `, `, 1,174 times. **Nine are this story** — three forms of `Lafond`, three of `Jamison`, `Nicholas`, `Cookie`, `ballroom` |
| **the dictionary** | **816 entries × 7 bytes, ending exactly on `0x4E00`**, the declared base of high memory. 3 separators, 144 verbs, 408 grammar lines, 26 prepositions |
| **the fourth closure test** | **it fails in both directions and that is correct.** 619 of 816 entries occur in the prose; **2,743 of 3,362** printed forms would be refused by the parser. A game that only printed what it could parse would have a vocabulary of 619 words; it has 3,705 |
| **the object tree** | **223 objects** — `(0x0C95 − 0x04BE) / 9`, remainder 0. **0 cycles, 0 orphans, 0 bad pointers, 0 asymmetries**, and **12 roots**, not the one the briefing asked for: parent 0 means *nowhere*, and ten things start the game out of play |
| **the memory map** | 19 regions over **128,963 bytes: 0 owned by nobody, 0 owned by two.** [12](docs/12-the-memory-map.md) |
| **the two bytes** | 240 globals from `0x02A2` end at `0x0482` and the object table starts at `0x0480`. The code references **239 of 240 globals, and the one it never touches is number 239** |
| **the code** | **614 routines, 13,856 instructions, 60 distinct opcodes.** A sound reachability walk sees **91** of the 614, because the parser calls its 183 action routines through a table |
| **printing** | 26.00 % of all instructions are instructions that say something. Arithmetic is **215 in 13,856** — one in sixty-four |
| **the thesis, at zero** | 82.93 % filmed, 77.81 % recorded, 46.44 % rendered — and here **0 bytes of audio, image, video, font or palette**, and `sound_effect` among the fourteen opcodes the game never issues |
| **the file that is not here** | `LEATHER.SCR`, in an 11-byte buffer, referenced by three instructions, reachable from the output path *and* the keyboard, guarded by `cmp al, 2`. First object in this branch where **a binary asks for a file that does not exist**. [14](docs/14-the-file-that-is-not-here.md) |
| **the copy check** | `Unauthorized copy` is referenced once, from a branch taken on the carry flag of a subroutine whose entire body is **`F8 C3` — clear carry, return**. The message can never appear, and this document says what would decide whether that was built or patched. [15](docs/15-the-copy-check.md) |
| **three bytes** | `SETUP.INF` is `PJY`: `P`−0x37−1 = **24 rows**, `J`−0xFA = **80 columns**, `Y` a flag. Opened **read-only**; nothing in these five files writes it. A real layer whose producer is absent |
| **absolute paths** | 0 · 0 · 0 · 0 · 101 · 31,737 · **0**. Measured three ways — the inherited tool unmodified, both path shapes per file, and a third pass **over the decoded text**, which no byte-level tool could do |
| **the leftovers** | **602 bytes, 0.4116 %**: six developer verbs including `zzmgck` and a `$ve` that runs the checksum, two grammar blocks nothing reaches, **20 nouns for things that are not in the game**, a filename for another title, a message that cannot be printed, and 160 bytes of software that still thinks it is on a floppy |
| **the predictions** | **66 clauses plus 6 named inferences, 84.85 %** — method 91.67 %, content 83.33 %. The highest yet, and [23](docs/23-prediction-scoring.md) says why that is not good news |

---

## The chapters

| | |
|---|---|
| [00 — the predictions](docs/00-predictions.md) | sixty-six bets placed before a byte was decoded |
| [01 — the object](docs/01-what-this-object-is.md) | five files, and 88 % of them is language |
| [02 — the spec sheet](docs/02-spec-sheet.md) | every number with the command that reproduces it, and the **Engine** |
| [03 — the header](docs/03-the-header.md) | the eighth answer to Q1, and the first one from 1987 |
| [04 — the clocks](docs/04-the-clocks.md) | two timestamps, fourteen years apart, and both of them wrong |
| [05 — the interpreter](docs/05-the-interpreter.md) | a virtual machine in 12,004 bytes that never says who wrote it |
| [06 — the alphabet](docs/06-the-alphabet.md) | derived from the data, then checked against the copy printed in the machine |
| [07 — the text](docs/07-the-text.md) | eighteen thousand seven hundred and one words |
| [08 — the abbreviations](docs/08-the-abbreviations.md) | ninety-six strings that save 12,158 bytes |
| [09 — the dictionary](docs/09-the-dictionary.md) | 816 entries, and the fourth closure test, which fails correctly |
| [10 — the object tree](docs/10-the-object-tree.md) | 223 objects, twelve roots, and no cycle |
| [11 — the parser's tables](docs/11-the-parser.md) | 144 verbs, 408 grammar lines, 366 routine addresses |
| [12 — the memory map](docs/12-the-memory-map.md) | 128,963 bytes, nothing unowned, nothing owned twice |
| [13 — the code](docs/13-the-code.md) | 614 routines, and the 523 a sound method cannot see |
| [14 — the file that is not here](docs/14-the-file-that-is-not-here.md) | a binary that asks for a file belonging to a different game |
| [15 — the copy check](docs/15-the-copy-check.md) | `Unauthorized copy`, and the two bytes that decide it |
| [16 — three bytes](docs/16-three-bytes.md) | `SETUP.INF`, and what the interpreter does with each of them |
| [17 — the driver](docs/17-the-driver.md) | 3.61 % of the object, by four other people |
| [18 — the absolute paths](docs/18-the-absolute-paths.md) | 0, 0, 0, 0, 101, 31,737, and then 0 again — measured three ways |
| [19 — the leftovers](docs/19-the-leftovers.md) | 602 bytes, and twenty nouns for things that are not there |
| [20 — the tools](docs/20-the-tools.md) | fifteen, of which nine were written here and three were run to be refused |
| [21 — open questions](docs/21-open-questions.md) | one answered, one carried, one not testable, and three new |
| [22 — corrections](docs/22-corrections.md) | twelve of mine, five of the briefing's |
| [23 — prediction scoring](docs/23-prediction-scoring.md) | 84.85 %, and the reason that is not good news |

---

## The question

One hundred and forty-six thousand bytes, five files, no image, no sound, and a
twelve-kilobyte virtual machine that refuses to say who wrote it. Eighty-eight
per cent of the object is language compressed by an algorithm designed when
memory cost more than time.

**How many words are really in there, how many were saved, and how many of these
bytes belong to somebody?**

**18,701 words.** **12,158 bytes saved**, by 96 strings that cost 610 to keep —
and nine of the 96 are the names of the people in the story, because a
compression table built for one book is a summary of that book.

And **all of them belong to somebody**: 128,963 bytes assigned to nineteen
regions with nothing unowned and nothing owned twice, 146,252 across five layers
with one row marked *inferred* and one marked *producer absent*. The only bytes
in the object whose owner is a real, named human being are 5,221 of console
driver by two people who never heard of this game — and the **110 bytes** that
carry `Copyright (c) 1987 by Infocom, Inc.` are five-bit characters no search
can see.

# Mega Man 3: The Robots are Revolting — PC/DOS, 1992

A byte-level study of the 277,214-byte ZIP that holds *Mega Man 3* for MS-DOS:
the container read as an object before it was opened, the twelve-bit LZW every
file in the game goes through, four undocumented formats, and the 1,855 bytes
this program shares with the same studio's 1990 *Mega Man*.

Nothing here is emulation, patching or preservation advocacy. It is
measurement: every number carries the command that reproduces it, the
predictions were written before the archive was extracted and are scored whether
they won or lost, and the formats are described in the docstrings of the tools
that read them.

It is also the first object in this collection with a **sibling already measured
to the byte**, and that changes what a chapter is for. Three open questions from
[`pc-megaman-doc`](https://github.com/vs-sr-dev/pc-megaman-doc) are closed here,
one of its tools is corrected here, and the one inference this document put
above all the others fell — because the two games' menu is byte-identical and
their pixel format is not.

---

## The short card

| | |
|---|---|
| **title** | *Mega Man 3: The Robots are Revolting* — there is no *Mega Man 2* for PC |
| **platform** | MS-DOS, CGA / EGA / Tandy, 320 × 200, sixteen colours. **No VGA**: the 1990 game offered it and this one dropped it |
| **year** | **1992** — 64 of 64 files dated 18 July to 2 August 1992, and `© 1992 CAPCOM` drawn in pixels on the title screen |
| **licensor** | **Capcom**, on `LOGO.STA` and in the credits, as pixels |
| **developer** | **Rozner Labs** — `A / ROZNER / LABS / PRODUCTION` on `ROZLABS.STA`, as pixels |
| **publisher** | **Hi Tech Expressions** — its logo and `PRESENTS` on `HITECHLO.STA`, as pixels |
| **credited** | **Stephen Rozner** (design, programming, sound) and **William Rozner** (graphics). In 1990 one name did all four jobs |
| **the container** | 65 ZIP records, 65 CRC-32s verified, 0 header disagreements, 0 extra fields — and a central directory a 2008 `sort` re-ordered |
| **the folder** | 64 files, 392,593 bytes, 64 distinct SHA-1s |
| **the executable** | 36,114 bytes, EXEPACK'd short-header; unpacks to 55,456 of which 40.8 % is zero. One segment, 24 relocations |
| **the rest of the code** | there is none. The 1990 game shipped 71 % of its code in five per-stage `.BIN` modules; **this one has no `.BIN` family** |
| **the codec** | **twelve-bit LZW**, MSB first, no clear code, dictionary frozen at 0xFFE — and it is in the executable at 0xb280, which is where the format was confirmed a second time |
| **the pixel** | **one byte per pixel, chunky**, sixteen colours. Not 1990's four EGA planes. Converted to planes once per tile at load time |
| **the palette** | the 1990 tables, byte for byte, sixteen bytes apart. Thirty-two bytes that did not move |
| **stages** | seven: `FCASTLE` 190 × 168, `FCITY` 300 × 86, `FOCEAN` 320 × 96, `FOILRIG` 188 × 98, `FREFINE` 196 × 99, `FSEWER` 315 × 78, `FTANKER` 235 × 104 tiles |
| **objects** | 366 sixteen-byte records in the `.ZSC` files — the enemy placement that used to be compiled code |
| **bosses** | six, named twice: as ASCII in the executable and as pixel plates in `BOSSSCRN.VFR`, in the same order |
| **tile** | 16 × 16 px = 256 bytes; a bank is **256 tiles + 256 records of 32 bytes + four 256-byte tables** = 74,752 |
| **sprites** | 326 frames in 43 banks, one file per drawn object; mask byte first, every eight pixels, exactly as in 1990 |
| **audio** | PC speaker only. No sound file, no sound chip touched |
| **shared with the 1990 game** | **1,855 bytes** of program, in runs of ≥ 32, including 98 bytes of the options menu and 32 of palette. The **Saga** cell fills |
| **leftovers** | 118,293 decoded bytes, costing 16,509 as shipped — **4.21 %**, against 9.89 % in 1990 |
| **predictions** | 53 clauses written before the zip was opened; 31 hit, 13 half, 9 miss = **70.8 %** |

Everything above is derived in the chapters and every figure has a command.

---

## The chapters

| | |
|---|---|
| [00 — the predictions](docs/00-predictions.md) | fifty-three bets placed before the archive was extracted, and the one inference four of them hung on |
| [01 — the archive](docs/01-what-this-archive-is.md) | sixty-four files, one container, and a game whose number is a lie |
| [02 — the spec sheet](docs/02-spec-sheet.md) | every number, with the command that reproduces it |
| [03 — the container](docs/03-the-container.md) | what a folder has instead of a volume descriptor, and the one field a `sort` destroys |
| [04 — EXEPACK](docs/04-exepack-and-the-image.md) | thirty-six thousand bytes that are not nine tenths air, and 627 that were in the wrong place |
| [05 — the codec and the pixel](docs/05-the-codec-and-the-pixel.md) | twelve-bit LZW, one byte a pixel, and a dictionary that runs out a third of the way through |
| [06 — inside the image](docs/06-inside-the-image.md) | a manifest that closes, a menu minus one option, and three ways to spell one name |
| [07 — `.ZSC`](docs/07-zsc-the-maps-and-the-objects.md) | seven maps, 366 objects, and the file that replaced a compiler |
| [08 — `.ZBL`](docs/08-zbl-the-tile-banks.md) | 256 tiles, 256 records, four tables — and the answer to somebody else's open question |
| [09 — `.VFR`](docs/09-vfr-the-frames.md) | forty-three files, 326 frames, and a hit box that used to be code |
| [10 — `.STA`](docs/10-sta-the-six-screens.md) | six screens, the same three letters, and everything else different |
| [11 — against 1990](docs/11-against-1990.md) | 1,855 shared bytes, and what a studio keeps when it throws everything else away |
| [12 — the clocks](docs/12-the-clocks.md) | fourteen days, ten runs, and twenty-one minutes where there used to be twenty-four days |
| [13 — against the collection](docs/13-against-the-collection.md) | the same problem, solved again, by somebody who had done it once |
| [14 — open questions](docs/14-open-questions.md) | eight things this document could not close, and three it closed for another one |
| [15 — the scoring](docs/15-prediction-scoring.md) | fifty-three bets, one wrong idea that cost four, and a sibling that was a trap in exactly one place |
| [16 — the tools](docs/16-tools.md) | thirteen scripts, and one bug found by being run somewhere new |
| [17 — leftovers](docs/17-leftovers.md) | 4.21 % of the object, after a draft that said 26.51 % |
| [18 — corrections](docs/18-corrections.md) | six errors in the briefing, five in this session's own work, one in a tool two repositories old |

---

## Running the tools

The tools expect the archive in the current directory and write everything they
produce into `_work/`, which is not in this repository. **No game asset, render
or extracted file is committed here** — this repository is text.

```
python tools/zipcensus.py Mega-Man-3-The-Robots-are-Revolting_DOS_EN.zip
python tools/zipcensus.py Mega-Man-3-The-Robots-are-Revolting_DOS_EN.zip --extract _work/game
python tools/clocks.py    Mega-Man-3-The-Robots-are-Revolting_DOS_EN.zip
python tools/exepack.py   _work/game/Mm.exe --out _work/mm.unpacked.bin
python tools/lzw.py --all _work/game          # every compressed file, decoded and checked
python tools/pixels.py    _work/mm.unpacked.bin
python tools/zsc.py --all _work/game --objects
python tools/zbl.py --all _work/game --recs
python tools/vfr.py --all _work/game --mask
python tools/sta.py --all _work/game --dir _work/render
python tools/crossmatch.py _work/exe _work/exe90 --raw --min 32
python tools/leftovers.py _work/game
python tools/toolclass.py tools
python tools/checkscore.py docs/15-prediction-scoring.md
```

Python 3. `Pillow` for anything that draws; `capstone` for the disassembly
(which uses `../pc-megaman-doc/tools/dis16.py`). The decoders, the closure
checks and the container census need neither.

---

## What this is part of

One of a set of independent studies of individual game releases, indexed at
[`pc-gamelist-doc`](https://github.com/vs-sr-dev/pc-gamelist-doc). Its direct
sibling is [`pc-megaman-doc`](https://github.com/vs-sr-dev/pc-megaman-doc) —
same studio, same programmer, same platform, twenty-one months earlier — and the
two are the only matched pair in the collection. The nearest neighbours in
method are [`pc-baronbaldric-doc`](https://github.com/vs-sr-dev/pc-baronbaldric-doc)
and [`pc-tubularworlds-doc`](https://github.com/vs-sr-dev/pc-tubularworlds-doc):
same branch, same shape of object — a DOS executable, proprietary extension
families, no installer.

# pc-corridor7-doc

Reverse-engineering notes on **Corridor 7: Alien Invasion**
(Capstone Software / IntraCorp, 1994) — the DOS shooter Capstone built on a
licensed Wolfenstein 3-D engine, and the one that ships its levels in TED5's
development format.

files and the four executables that install alongside them. The later
Steam/GOG re-release is out of scope.

committed here. The tools in [`tools/`](tools/) reproduce every figure, table
and image from your own legally obtained copy.

| [06-end-sequence.md](docs/06-end-sequence.md) | `SEQTWO.CO7` is a plain `.FLC`; `AUDIOSEQ.CO7` and `EXPUNGE.EXE` |
| [07-config-and-saves.md](docs/07-config-and-saves.md) | `CONFIG.DAT`, `SAVEGAM?.CO7`, `AUTOSAVE.DAT`, `EZI.HST` |
| [08-vs-wolfenstein.md](docs/08-vs-wolfenstein.md) | What came across unchanged, what was extended, what was replaced |

| [11-palettes.md](docs/11-palettes.md) | The three VGA palettes in `C7.EXE`, how the game palette is built, and the one picture with a palette of its own |
| [10-open-questions.md](docs/10-open-questions.md) | Everything unresolved, with the measurements behind it |
| [notes/music-timeline.md](notes/music-timeline.md) | All 34 tracks, dated from their MUSE tags |
| [notes/level-inventory.md](notes/level-inventory.md) | All 36 levels, per-plane sizes and tile counts |

## Highlights

**It really is Wolfenstein 3-D underneath, and the game says so.** The
copyright screen credits "Portions of the program (c) 1994 Id Software", and
id's RLEW, Huffman, page-file, compiled-shape, MUSE and TED5 formats all read
without modification. What Capstone changed is the top half: 256-colour art
throughout, a second page file for digitised sound, a wider tile space, and a
pre-rendered `.FLC` ending.

**The shipped maps are the editor's work file.** `MAPTEMP.CO7` opens with
`TED5v1.0` and its planes are RLEW-compressed and nothing else — no Carmack
layer, no `GAMEMAPS`. The 100-entry map directory is linked into `C7.EXE` at
0x24BF0, which is why no `MAPHEAD.CO7` ships. One level, number 27, sits at
the very end of the file, after the secret levels: the one TED5 had to
re-append.

**The soundtrack can be dated to the day.** Every music chunk keeps an 88-byte
MUSE tag with its source file name and a packed MS-DOS date/time. The 34
tracks run from `TESTB.IMF` on 12 January 1994 to `L3LOOP.IMF` on 25 March
1994 — the same day the data files were built. Working titles and all:
`BTMLIK`, `SLAY1`, `COORSLOW`, `TGRUV`, and a `LEVEL1`/`2`/`3`/`5` with no
`LEVEL4`.

**The credits are a corridor.** Thirteen of the 598 sprites are the credit
roll drawn as artwork, and ten of them are placed as static objects along the
western corridor of level 1 — at `x = 2`, every three tiles, from `y = 2` to
`y = 29`. The player spawns facing the other way.

**A Star Trek dedication wall.** Four wall textures near the end of the set
are display plaques: `WHERE NO ONE HAS GONE BEFORE`, `NCC-1701D`, the United
Federation of Planets emblem, and the blank plaque the other three were drawn
over. Nine tiles on level 2 use them, and nowhere else in the game.

**Three palettes, and none of them a tint.** `C7.EXE` holds exactly three
768-byte VGA palettes. The game one — 768 bytes at 0x23E70, located by the
grey ramp that lands on palette index 32 — is a designed artist's palette:
16 fixed colours, then **nine 24-step hue ramps**, then 24 HUD colours. The
second keeps that skeleton and collapses all nine ramps to one red ramp, and
it is demonstrably authored rather than generated: 123 of its entries have
*less* red than the game palette, which no shift toward red can produce. The
third fits exactly one asset in the whole game.

## Tools

Pure Python 3. `pillow` and `numpy` are needed only for the rendering paths.

```
tools/c7lib.py      Game paths, RLEW, Huffman, Mode-X unmunge, palette, DOS dates
tools/c7pages.py    GFXTILES.CO7 walls and compiled sprites
tools/c7gfx.py      VGAGRAPH pictures, fonts and text pages
tools/c7maps.py     MAPTEMP.CO7 levels, census and texture-accurate plans
tools/c7audio.py    AUDIOT chunks, IMF songs and tags, AUDIOMUS digitised bank
tools/c7flic.py     SEQTWO.CO7 FLIC decoder and AUDIOSEQ.CO7
tools/c7cfg.py      CONFIG.DAT and the save files
tools/c7export.py   one shot: everything above into one directory
```

```sh
python tools/c7export.py "<install>" ./out
```

or piecemeal:

```sh
python tools/c7pages.py "<install>" walls   ./walls
python tools/c7gfx.py   "<install>" text
python tools/c7maps.py  "<install>" dump 0
python tools/c7audio.py "<install>" timeline
python tools/c7flic.py  "<install>" info
python tools/c7cfg.py   "<install>" verify "<install>/AUTOSAVE.DAT" 1
```

`<install>` is the directory holding `C7.EXE` and the `*.CO7` files.

## Status

First pass. Chapter 10 lists what is still open — chiefly the exact door
code-to-texture binding, the meaning of the plane-1 wall flags 99–107, the
orphaned `GFXINFOV.CO7`, and the `BLORCH` and `SEQONE` ghosts. Nothing in the
other chapters depends on those answers.

# pc-teenagent-doc

A measured description of one directory: 433 files, 93,184,691 bytes, as
GOG Galaxy wrote them to disk on 2026-09-11, holding **TEENAGENT**
(Metropolis Software House, MS-DOS, `(c) 1994-1995`; published by Union
Logic Software Publishing Inc. of Nepean, Ontario — all of it read out of
the object's own bytes, none of it from outside) inside DOSBox Staging and
GOG's storefront. The game is fifteen of the files and 16.5 % of the bytes.
The object is not published. What is published is what could be counted,
unpacked, decoded, rendered and checked — and this time the packer had
erased its own name and the words were behind it.

## The short card

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **what it is** | a mouse-driven point-and-click adventure: Mark, a rookie, after disappearing gold, through 42 painted rooms — delivered inside a GOG Galaxy install of which it is 16.5 %, with **the 16.4 % that is its twelve `.RES` containers opened this session to the last of 1,053 members** |
| **studio** | Metropolis Software House — `production / METROPOLIS SOFTWARE HOUSE` in the unpacked engine's credit roll; `(c) Metropolis 1994` in the unpacked `SOUNDSET.EXE`; painted in `VARIA.RES`; typed on the registered-version exit screen; address *ul. M.C. Skłodowskiej 92, 59-300 Lubin* on advert page 10. Programming and script Adrian Chmielarz, animation Grzegorz Miechowski, backgrounds Andrzej Dobrzyński, music Radek Szamrej |
| **year** | 1994–1995 — `(c) 1994-1995` printed by the program; *Coming spring 1995!* painted on advert page 11; 1994 on the eight sound drivers and the sound setup |
| **publisher** | Union Logic Software Publishing Inc., Nepean, Ontario, Canada — on two text-mode order screens, eleven advert pages and a logo screen; the registered-version screen says *copyrighted by Union Logic Software Publishing, Inc. & Metropolis Software House* |
| **platform** | IBM PC, VGA 320 × 200 × 256, mouse; eight sound drivers (GUS, AdLib, SB, SB Pro, PC Speaker, none, SB DMA, Covox); delivered through DOSBox Staging 0.82.2 |
| **files** | 433 in 34 directories; the game 15 (12 `.RES`, 2 `.EXE`, `SOUND.SET`); DOSBox 393; GOG 25 |
| **bytes** | 93,184,691 — game 15,392,150 (16.5179 %), DOSBox 36,580,902 (39.2563 %), GOG 41,211,639 (44.2258 %, of which one 38 MB "Game Configurator" undeclared in GOG's manifest) |
| **distinct sha1** | 416 |
| **the clocks** | six, none the game's: 1994 (drivers), 2017/2019 (GOG icons), 2025-06-17 (DOSBox source), 2025-11-06 (the packager's two shipped logs), 2025-11-19 (GOG's build), 2026-09-11 (the install); the game's own is the printed 1994–1995 |
| **coverage** | specified 80.6898 %, derived 16.4292 % (the twelve `.RES`), opaque 2.8811 %, residue 0 |
| **the program** | `TEENAGNT.EXE` 78,426 B, LZEXE 0.91 with the `LZ91` marker replaced by `0C 0A 09 01` and `*FAB*` still in the stub; unpacked by `lzexe.py` from the stub's disassembly to 152,434 B, 39 relocations, closing; `SOUNDSET.EXE` the same |
| **the words** | 656 messages, 1,217 lines, 4,338 words in the unpacked data segment — none in any `.RES` |
| **the containers** | 12 directories closing on their lengths; 1,053 members: 54 screens (42 rooms, 11 advert pages, a logo), 586 animations, 124 sprites, 31 overlays (Mark, 92 items), 88 empty slots, 2 fonts with the Polish alphabet on the punctuation slots, 2 exit screens, 11 song headers, 144 signed 8-bit samples, 8 drivers |
| **crossings** | 4 of 416 hashes over 114 repositories — all four GOG's installer furniture; no game file, no DOSBox file |
| **tools** | 592 Python files: 589 inherited (4 changed), 3 written |

**The work this time was two readers and the words between them.** The
program's entry stub was disassembled whole — 330 bytes, 168 instructions,
every byte decoded — and `lzexe.py` was written from that listing: a
16-bit bit buffer, three match shapes, a delta-coded relocation list, an
entry taken from the stub's first eight bytes. Out came a data segment
with every line the game says, from *Life is brutal.* to *I hope all this
fish stuff is not a red herring.*, and a credit roll that closed the two
cells the pre-briefing had left open. Then the twelve containers: their
directory is twenty lines, and the engine's loader reads it the same way;
their members are five grammars read out of the engine's blitter, its
animation stepper and one sound driver — screens with a trailing 6-bit
palette, sprites at screen offsets with FFh transparent, per-room
overlays, animations as step lists over frame tables, glyphs of 0/1/2 —
each closing on every member it claims. Out came the game: a farm, a lake,
a mansion with a library and a vault, a *MEGABANK*, a hen that walks and
flaps in 40 frames, Mark in a red shirt, 92 things to pick up, and a font
that still spells *Dobrzyński* the Polish way.

**The pre-briefing was wrong six times**, each caught by a byte:
`SOUNDSET.EXE` is packed too; *Metropolis* is in four game files; the
header offset it quoted was one row up; the advert pages are not the
title; the year is printed after all; and one of the session's own
sentences claimed a confirmation the owner had not yet given (it came
after, on all 54 renders). Its five
hunches score four true in the main and one half, with the samples signed
where it said unsigned.

## The chapters

Seven, and the count is the content's. One for the program, because the
packer is the gate to the words; one for the words, because they are the
game; one for the twelve containers, because they are the 16.4 %; one for
the shop and the emulator together, because they are 83.5 % of the bytes
and none of the game; and no chapter for the engine, which was
disassembled exactly as far as the formats needed.

| chapter | the sentence |
|---|---|
| [01 — What this is](docs/01-what-this-is.md) | a 15 MB adventure inside a 93 MB shop: the object, the split, the coverage, the denominators |
| [02 — The technical sheet](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | every figure with the command that re-derives it |
| [03 — The program](docs/03-the-packer-that-erased-its-name.md) | a packer that erased its name, read from its own stub and removed; `dospack.py` repaired |
| [04 — The words](docs/04-the-words.md) | 4,338 of them in the data segment; the credits, the studio, the year, the Polish font map |
| [05 — Twelve containers](docs/05-twelve-containers.md) | 1,053 members, every one named by a grammar that closes: rooms, adverts, sprites, animations, Mark, items, fonts, exit screens, music heads, samples, drivers |
| [06 — The shop and the emulator](docs/06-the-shop-and-the-emulator.md) | 83.5 % of the bytes, 0 % of the game; the six clocks; the CD image that was there and is not here |
| [07 — Corrections, predictions and calibration](docs/07-corrections-predictions-and-calibration.md) | six corrections, five hunches scored, one term, rule 0 as a program |

## The rules this was written under

The object is not run, not installed, not emulated — a DOSBox is in it and
was not launched. Unpacking LZEXE by reading its stub and decoding the
containers are reading bytes as data. **The famous free implementation of
this game's engine was not opened, read, quoted or consulted to check a
result**; what the pre-briefing recalled of it was tested against the bytes
and nothing more. Every figure names its denominator and the command that
re-derives it; every reader refuses a directory, prints a non-Latin-1 name
safely, selects by magic, and passes its selftest in a repository that
does not hold the object or says what it skipped. The documents are in
English; the sessions were in Italian.

# pc-bumpy-doc

A measured description of one folder: 57 files, 743,759 bytes, 0
subdirectories, copied from the owner's drive as a 1992 download directory
holding **BUMPY'S ARCADE FANTASY** (MS-DOS; `BUMPY (C) LORICIEL 1992`
printed by its own program and painted with the studio's panther on its
presentation screen) — a French bouncing-ball arcade in nine levels of
fifteen or twelve platforms, wrapped in a Fairlight release of 18 July 1992
with its NFO, the NFO's blank form, a BBS advert, an anti-virus receipt,
a 2-byte disk key and three empty files that spell a board. The program is
not packed and says almost nothing; every picture and every level sits
behind a 12-byte head whose length is big-endian on a PC, and two level
files were left in the clear as the key. The object is not published.
What is published is what could be counted, read out of the loader,
unpacked, rendered and checked — all of it from the object's own bytes,
none of it from outside.

## The short card

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **what it is** | a platform arcade of a red ball with eyes and blue gloves, bouncing across screens of platforms — bars, springs, spiked bars, broken ones — collecting fruit and gifts among monsters; nine worlds (teddy bears and balloons, hedgehogs in sunglasses …), each a map of rings joined by paths, each a `.BUM/.DEC/.PAV` triple of 15 or 12 platforms on 8 × 6 grids; a password per level and a copy protection that asks for a platform number from the manual — cracked in two bytes |
| **title** | BUMPY'S ARCADE FANTASY — painted with the apostrophe on `TITRE.VEC` and `BUMPRESE.VEC`; `BUMPY` in the program's two menus and its file names; Fairlight typed `BUMPY ARCADE FANTASY` |
| **studio** | **Loriciel** — `BUMPY (C) LORICIEL 1992` at 1684Ch and 17DF0h of `BUMPY.EXE`, the video and sound menus; the panther and the word `LORICIEL` painted on the presentation screen; Fairlight's `Loreciel` is a misspelling. The people, painted on the last screen: *auteur* JF Streife, *programmation* F Spada, M Winogradoff, *musique* C Perrotin, *graphisme* I Maury, P Jarry, and `R.D` |
| **year** | 1992 — the copyright line in the program, twice; the release 1992-07-18 by its NFO; twelve files dated June–July 1992; seventeen dated 1987-04-22 by a clock, twenty-four by a broken one (2052, 2055) |
| **language** | French — the installer (`Insérez la disquette`, `Bon amusement`), the joystick errors (`Erreur dans TstJoy`), the file names (`MONDE`, `TITRE`, `DESSFIN`, `FLECHE`, `BUMSPJEU`), the credits (`AUTEUR`, `GRAPHISME`); the game's own texts English (`ENTER YOUR PASSWORD`, `HALL OF FAME`, `EASY / MEDIUM / HARD`) |
| **platform** | IBM PC, 8086 code, Turbo C++ 1990; CGA/EGA/VGA/Tandy/MCGA/VGA256 offered, EGA and VGA in BIOS mode 0Dh 320 × 200 × 16; Ad Lib (OPL2 at 388h) and MT-32 (MPU-401 at 330h); joystick (201h) and mouse (`int 33h`); two floppies, `a` and `b`, or a hard disk with `QUELDISK` = `z` |
| **files** | 57: 14 `.VEC` screens, 9 × `.BUM/.DEC/.PAV` levels, 2 sprite banks, 1 font, 1 MIDI, 1 Ad Lib bank, 1 program, 2 batches, 2 NFOs, 1 TheDraw `.COM`, 1 CPAV checklist, `QUELDISK`, 3 empty |
| **bytes** | 743,759 — behind the 12-byte head 443,827 (59.67 %, 38 files → 812,935 unpacked), program 112,704, sprites 91,304, MIDI 35,141, `SCORE.VEC` 32,099, release 14,209, bank 6,748, the two plaintext levels 5,242, font 1,981, installer and `QUELDISK` 504 |
| **distinct sha1** | 55 — the empty file three times |
| **the head** | `u32 BE` unpacked length, `u32 BE` unused, `u16 BE` method (4 = RLE with escape, 12 = bit mask over the output; bit 15 = last stage), `u16 BE` XOR of the five; read out of the module at 0C28h:0000 with `dosdis.py`; **38 of 38 close**, up to three stages deep (93 in all), and the two plaintext `.BUM` are the shapes they close on |
| **the screens** | 14 × 32,099 = 51 zero bytes + 48 DAC bytes (6-bit, into DAC 0–7 and 16–23) + four planes of 8,000; title, presentation with the panther, credits, difficulty overlay, nine worlds, the *HALL OF FAME* frame — all fourteen confirmed by the owner |
| **the game** | 126 platforms: 194-byte records of three 8 × 6 tables (a floor row of eight 1s, a staircase diagonal) + 6 parameters; 812-byte décor records of 270 triplets; 320 × 192 four-plane backgrounds; 511 sprites (40 sizes, 16 × 16 to 48 × 27) behind a 512-entry big-endian table with 12-byte heads *below* the pointers; a 7 × 8 font of 86 glyphs padded to even addresses; eight passwords; seven default scores from 5,000,000 down to 500 |
| **the protection** | `Enter the platform number`: a random sprite from a 16-entry table, the manual's number from another (4, 6, 7, 5, 15 …), three tries — and at cs:4219 the entered number is written over the expected one and a `jmp` skips the `ERROR` branch nothing else reaches: `88 46 FC EB 1D` where `3A 46 FC 74 1D` would compare; no disk check anywhere (`int 13h` ×0) |
| **the music** | `BUMPY.MID` SMF 1, 7 tracks (`xylo`, `harpsi`, `bass2`, `bells`, `pompe`, `programs`), 192 ppqn, 75 bpm, 3,863 notes, ≈ 3′45″; `BUMPY.BNK` Ad Lib v1.0, 129 of 160 instruments named `rol000..rol128_` |
| **the release** | Fairlight, `Cracked By: Sleepwalker`, `Packaged By: Grimstalk`, 07/18/92; `FLT.BAK` the form with the fields blank (261 bytes differ); `LIMITS.COM` = *The Outer Limits BBS, Fairlight Member Board, 313*, the board the NFO lists with SysOp FlashBack; `CHKLIST.CPS` CPAV's record of this `BUMPY.EXE`, 07-17; `BIO-TECH'S WORLD` in three file names |
| **crossings** | 0 of 55 over 116 repositories |
| **coverage** | specified 22.7597 %, derived 77.2403 %, opaque 0 bytes (3 empty files), residue 0 — from 78.36 % opaque and two NFOs filed as Shift-JIS before this session |
| **tools** | 605 Python files: 598 inherited (1 repaired: `coverage.py`'s cp437 probe, fourth appearance of its defect), 7 written — five readers from listings, a MIDI walker and a bank census |

**The work this time was one decompressor, one blitter read as far as its
palette, five readers, one repair — and a program that would not speak
until its loader was followed.** The codec was read whole: a head reader
that swaps every word, a dispatcher that loops while bit 15 is clear, and
two handlers out of eighteen — run-length behind an escape, and a bit mask
that writes one chosen byte where a flag is set. Out came fourteen screens,
and the first render decided sequential planes over interleaved ones; out
came the title with its apostrophe, the panther, and a credits screen the
owner had never reached. Then the program gave up what the pre-briefing
had missed in its own string dump — `BUMPY (C) LORICIEL 1992`, twice — and
what nobody had asked: a loader keyed to two floppies by a 2-byte file, a
resource table with five files nothing opens, a copy protection built on
the manual's platform numbers, and the two bytes that turn its comparison
into an assignment.

**The pre-briefing's figures were corrected twelve times**, from 70 % to
59.67 % for the headed bytes to "no studio, no year in the program". Its
five hunches score three halves, a third and a sixth, and no whole truth.

## The chapters

Eight, and the count is the content's: the codec had to be one because it
is 60 % of the bytes and every picture; the screens one because the title
and the studio are pixels; the game one because the owner played it and
the levels are what they never saw; the program one because the protection,
the crack and the two-disk loader are its story; the release and the
clocks one because a download directory of 1992 is its own object; and
the tools one because a repair came before the first reader.

| chapter | what it says |
|---|---|
| [01 — What this is](docs/01-what-this-is.md) | the folder, the split, what the object says in the clear, the denominators, coverage |
| [02 — The technical sheet](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | every figure with its command |
| [03 — The codec](docs/03-the-codec.md) | the 12-byte head, the dispatcher, method 4 and method 12, the closure on 38 of 38 and on the two plaintexts |
| [04 — The screens](docs/04-the-screens.md) | the layout from the blitter and the palette loader, the fourteen renders, the title that names the game and the panther that names the studio |
| [05 — The game](docs/05-the-game.md) | nine levels in three files each, 126 platforms, the 8 × 6 grids, the backgrounds, 511 sprites, the font |
| [06 — The program](docs/06-the-program.md) | the strings, the two record tables and two floppies, `QUELDISK`, the copy protection and its two bytes, the ports |
| [07 — The release and the clocks](docs/07-the-release-and-the-clocks.md) | Fairlight's NFO and form, *The Outer Limits*, CPAV, the empty names, the MIDI and the bank, seven clocks, zero crossings |
| [08 — Tools, predictions and calibration](docs/08-tools-predictions-and-calibration.md) | the cp437 repair, the seven tools, rule 0, the five hunches scored, twelve corrections, the term +9.00 |

## Tools

605 Python files in `tools\`; the seven of this object and the repaired one:

| tool | reads | closes on |
|---|---|---|
| `bumpack.py` | the 12-byte compressed head, methods 4 and 12, stacked stages | the XOR check on every head, the declared length of every stage, 38 of 38 |
| `vecscreen.py` | the 32,099-byte screen: 51 + 48 palette bytes, four planes | DAC bytes ≤ 63, registers into DAC 0–7/16–23, exactly 32,099 |
| `bumsprite.py` | the 512-entry big-endian table, 12-byte heads below the pointers | table + heads + pixels + slack = file, offsets rising, h4 a multiple of 4 |
| `carfont.py` | the `.CAR` font: 224 absolute offsets, glyphs padded EVEN | the first offset = the table's end, every record 3 + (8 − top) + pad, residue 0 |
| `bumlevel.py` | `.BUM` 2 + n × 194, `.DEC` 2 + n × 812, `.PAV` 6 + 4 × 7,680 | the three lengths; prints the 8 × 6 grids; renders the backgrounds |
| `midiwalk.py`, `adlibbnk.py` | Standard MIDI (running status, meta, text names), the Ad Lib bank | the chunk walk on the file; 28 + 12n + 30n on the file |
| `coverage.py` | + `_cp437_text`, `_cp437_art` repaired; + 9 probes for this object | 187 selftest checks |

Every tool has a `selftest` on built specimens, refuses a directory
through `dirguard`, and prints names through `nameguard`. `notes\` holds
the output of every command the chapters cite; the renders stay in
`_work\` and are described, not published.

## Provenance

The folder arrived as a copy of the owner's, modification times kept; its
location is not written here. `INSTALL.BAT` says `C:\BUMPY`, and that is
the object's. Nothing outside the object was consulted — not Loriciel's
history, not another platform's version, not a recording of the levels
the owner never reached. What the bytes do not say, these documents say
they do not.

# Tubular Worlds — a folder, measured

A downloaded directory of 107 files, 3,432,758 bytes: an MS-DOS game of 1994,
German, with nineteen people named inside its own executable and no company
named anywhere. It is the thirteenth subject measured in this collection and
**the first that is not a medium** — no volume descriptor, no lead-out, no
sector, no second catalogue, and therefore no field anywhere that says when it
was made or where it stops.

Everything below is measured from the bytes. Each chapter opens with the
measurement it rests on, and every figure in the spec sheet carries the command
that reproduces it.

---

## The short sheet

| | |
|---|---|
| what it is | a folder on NTFS, 107 files in 8 directories — not a copy of a medium |
| bytes | **3,432,758** |
| distinct sha1 | **106** of 107; the one pair is `LEVEL0.COL` = `LEVEL1.COL`, 288 B |
| file dates | 1993-10-11 .. 1994-05-31, **231 days**, 60 of 107 files in January 1994 |
| how the copy was made | restored from a DOS-era archive: **107 of 107 mtimes on the MS-DOS two-second grid**, 107 of 107 with a zero sub-second field, 107 of 107 created on this volume *after* they were modified |
| files with an internal clock | **0** — the population, counted before anything was said about dates |
| the boundary | **106 of 107 files reachable from `TUBWORLD.BAT`**; the 107th is `TUBWORLD.BAT` |
| target | MS-DOS real mode, 16-bit MZ; no NE, no PE, no extender, nothing packed |
| compiler | **not recoverable** — no banner in either game executable, 2 and 10 relocations, whole-register prologues |
| video | VGA mode 13h for the game, mode 12h for the loading screens |
| the tile | **8 × 8 pixels, 64 bytes**, and a dense index range of **0..2639** with no gaps |
| keyboard | a 58-byte scancode table, **German QWERTZ**, compiled into both game programs |
| against the collection | **0 crossings** in 23,631 file records from eight published lists and ten working trees |
| bytes structured | **85.447 %** |
| bytes decoded | **74.383 %** |
| leftovers | **9,043 bytes, 0.263 %** |

**What is in it:** a scrolling shoot-'em-up in eight worlds, one or two
players — twenty-one level grids, sixteen object grids, fifteen tile banks, thirteen sprite banks,
thirteen songs, fourteen palettes, two loading screens in Deluxe Paint's IFF,
three programs, one batch file, and one person's high score.

---

## The chapters

| | |
|---|---|

| [01 — What this copy is](docs/01-what-this-copy-is.md) | a folder is not the work, and three timestamps that say how it got here |
